claims.text: The relatively low hardness and strength of single-phase equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are governed by intrinsically low lattice distortion.
Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni have similar atomic sizes and bonding characteristics.
Low lattice distortion in CoCrFeNiTi permits facile dislocation glide.
Facile glide and early-stage dynamic recovery produce minimal forest hardening in CoCrFeNiTi.
Ti promotes ductility in CoCrFeNiTi through its influence on stacking-fault energy.
Ti does not introduce enough atomic-size mismatch in CoCrFeNiTi to substantially impede dislocation motion.
HEAs containing elements with larger atomic-radius differences develop lattice strain that pins dislocations, raises strength and hardness, and reduces ductility.
The baseline comparator is an equimolar or nearly equimolar, homogeneous, single-phase CoCrFeNiTi solid solution.
Adding approximately 5 at.% Zr to CoCrFeNiTi will increase atomic-size mismatch.
The Zr-modified alloy will exhibit greater localized lattice-strain fields than the baseline alloy.
The Zr-modified alloy may develop short-range chemical order that hinders dislocation glide.
Minimal lattice distortion in baseline CoCrFeNiTi produces a low Peierls barrier for dislocation motion.
Local lattice strains introduced by Zr act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Relative to baseline CoCrFeNiTi, the approximately 5 at.% Zr alloy will have higher hardness and yield or compressive strength.
Relative to baseline CoCrFeNiTi, the approximately 5 at.% Zr alloy will have lower plastic strain.
The predicted strengthening and ductility reduction should be detectable from approximately 25 °C through 600 °C under quasi-static loading.

The hypothesis is limited to homogeneous, single-phase solid solutions and may fail when secondary phases, severe segregation, phase transformations, high strain rates, or dominant recovery processes occur.
A lack of statistically significant strengthening and corresponding evidence of dislocation pinning after increasing lattice distortion would falsify the proposed mechanism.
Unchanged ductility despite a measurable increase in lattice distortion would falsify the predicted strength-ductility tradeoff.
